title: VIII. The Third And Last Interview With Smerdyakov
paragraphs: Halfway there, the sharp dry wind that had blown early that morning picked up again, and a fine, dry snow came down thick and fast. It did not stay on the ground. The wind whirled it about, and before long it was a proper snowstorm. In that part of town, where Smerdyakov lived, there were hardly any street lamps. Ivan strode along alone in the dark. He paid no attention to the storm and found his way by instinct. His head ached, and his temples throbbed painfully. His hands, he noticed, were twitching convulsively. Close to Marya Kondratyevna’s cottage he ran into a lone drunken peasant, a small man in a coarse, patched coat. The man was zigzagging along, muttering and cursing to himself. Then, every so often, he would burst into song in a hoarse, drunken voice:
“Ach, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg; I won’t wait till he’s back.”

But every time he got as far as the second line he stopped and started cursing again, and then he began the same song from the top. Ivan hated him fiercely before he had even given him a thought. Then, all at once, he noticed the man and felt an irresistible urge to knock him down. At that moment they met. The peasant lurched violently and fell full tilt against Ivan, who shoved him back in a fury. The peasant flew backward and dropped like a log onto the frozen ground. He let out one pitiful “O—oh!” and then went quiet. Ivan stepped over to him. He lay on his back, not moving, quite unconscious. “He’ll freeze,” thought Ivan, and he went on to Smerdyakov’s.

In the passage, Marya Kondratyevna ran out with a candle in her hand to open the door. She whispered that Smerdyakov was very ill. “It’s not that he’s in bed, but he doesn’t seem himself. He even told us to take the tea away. He wouldn’t touch it.”
“What, does he make a row?” asked Ivan roughly.
“Oh, dear, no, it’s quite the opposite. He’s very quiet. Only please don’t talk to him for long,” Marya Kondratyevna begged him. Ivan opened the door and went into the room.

The room was as stuffy as before, but some things had changed. One of the benches along the wall had been taken out. In its place stood a big old mahogany sofa upholstered in leather, with a bed made up on it and fairly clean white pillows. Smerdyakov sat on the sofa in the same dressing-gown. The table had been pulled out in front of the sofa, so there was hardly any room to move. A thick book in a yellow cover lay on it, but Smerdyakov wasn’t reading. He seemed to be sitting there doing nothing at all. He met Ivan with a slow, silent look and didn’t appear surprised that he had come. His face had changed a great deal. He was much thinner and more sallow, his eyes were sunken, and there were blue shadows under them.
“Why, you really are ill?” Ivan stopped short. “I won’t keep you long. I won’t even take my coat off. Where can I sit?”
He went around to the far end of the table, pulled up a chair and sat down.
“Why are you staring at me and not saying anything? I’ve come with just one question, and I swear I’m not leaving without an answer. Has Katerina Ivanovna, the young lady, been to see you?”
Smerdyakov kept silent, looking quietly at Ivan as before. Then, with a wave of his hand, he suddenly turned his face away.
“What’s wrong with you?” cried Ivan.
“Nothing.”
“What do you mean, ‘nothing’?”
“Yes, she has. It’s none of your concern. Leave me alone.”
“No, I won’t leave you alone. Tell me, when was she here?”

“Why, I’d clean forgotten about her,” said Smerdyakov with a scornful smile. He turned his face back to Ivan and stared at him with a look of frenzied hatred, the same look he had given him at their last interview, a month before.
“You look very ill yourself, you know. Your face is sunken. You don’t look like yourself,” he said to Ivan.
“Never mind my health. Answer what I ask.”
“But why are your eyes so yellow? The whites are all yellow. Are you so worried?” He smiled with contempt and suddenly laughed out loud.
“Listen! I told you, I’m not going without an answer!” Ivan cried, hugely irritated.
“Why do you keep pestering me? Why do you torment me?” said Smerdyakov, looking pained.
“Damn it! I’ve nothing to do with you. Answer my question and I’ll be gone.”
“I’ve got no answer for you,” said Smerdyakov, looking down again.
“Don’t worry, I’ll make you answer!”

“Why are you so on edge?” Smerdyakov stared at him with more than contempt now. It was close to disgust. “Is it because the trial starts tomorrow? Nothing will happen to you. Can’t you believe that, at long last? Go home, go to bed and sleep in peace. Don’t be afraid of anything.”
“I don’t understand you.... What have I got to be afraid of tomorrow?” Ivan said in astonishment, and suddenly a cold breath of fear really did pass over his soul. Smerdyakov looked him over.
“You don’t understand?” he drawled, as if hurt. “Strange, that a man of sense would care to act out such a farce!”
Ivan stared at him, speechless. The man had once been his valet, and this astonishingly lofty tone was extraordinary in itself. He had not used such a tone even at their last interview.

“I tell you, you’ve nothing to be afraid of. I won’t say a word about you. There’s no proof against you. Look how your hands are shaking! Why are your fingers moving like that? Go home. It wasn’t _you_ who murdered him.”
Ivan started. He thought of Alyosha.
“I know it wasn’t me,” he faltered.
“Do you?” Smerdyakov pounced on him again.
Ivan leapt up and grabbed him by the shoulder.
“Tell me everything, you viper! Everything!”
Smerdyakov wasn’t the least bit scared. He simply fixed his eyes on Ivan with a mad hatred.
“Well, it was you who murdered him, if that’s how it is,” he whispered, furious.
Ivan dropped back onto his chair as if he were turning something over in his mind. He gave a nasty laugh.
“You mean my going away. What you were talking about last time?”
“Last time you stood right here in front of me, and you understood everything. You understand it now.”
“What I understand is that you’re mad.”

“Aren’t you sick of it? Here we are, face to face. What’s the use of keeping up this farce with each other? Are you still trying to pin it all on me, to my face? _You_ murdered him. You’re the real murderer. I was only your tool, your faithful servant, and I did it by your word.”
“_Did_ it? You mean you killed him?” Ivan went cold.
Something seemed to give way in his brain, and a cold shudder ran through him. Then Smerdyakov himself looked at him in wonder. Ivan’s horror was so real, it seems, that it struck him.
“You can’t mean you honestly didn’t know?” he faltered, distrustful, searching Ivan’s eyes with a forced smile. Ivan kept staring at him and seemed unable to speak.
Ach, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg; I won’t wait till he’s back,
rang out suddenly in his head.
“Do you know, I’m afraid you’re a dream, a ghost sitting here in front of me,” he muttered.
“There’s no ghost here. There’s just the two of us, and one more. He must be here, that third one, between us.”
“Who is he? Who’s here? What third person?” Ivan cried in alarm, looking about and hastily searching every corner with his eyes.
“That third one is God Himself—Providence. He’s the third beside us now. Only don’t look for Him. You won’t find Him.”
“It’s a lie that you killed him!” Ivan cried wildly. “You’re mad, or you’re teasing me again!”

Smerdyakov kept watching him with curiosity, as before, showing no fear. He still couldn’t quite shake off his disbelief. He still thought Ivan knew everything and was trying to “pin it all on him, to his face.”

“Wait a minute,” he said at last in a weak voice. He suddenly pulled his left leg out from under the table and began to roll up the trouser leg. He wore long white stockings and slippers. Slowly he undid his garter and groped down to the bottom of the stocking. Ivan watched, and suddenly he shuddered with a fit of terror.

“He’s mad!” he cried. He sprang up and backed away so fast that he knocked his back against the wall, and there he stood, pressed against it, stiff and straight. He stared in crazed terror at Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov paid no attention to his terror. He went on fumbling in his stocking, as if he were trying to catch hold of something with his fingers and draw it out. At last he got hold of it and started pulling it out. Ivan saw that it was a piece of paper, or maybe a roll of papers. Smerdyakov drew it out and laid it on the table.
“There,” he said quietly.
“What is it?” Ivan asked, trembling.
“Be so kind as to look at it,” Smerdyakov answered, still in the same low voice.
Ivan stepped up to the table, picked up the roll of paper and began to unfold it. Then he suddenly jerked his fingers away, as if he had touched some loathsome reptile.
“Your hands keep twitching,” Smerdyakov remarked, and he unfolded the bundle himself, unhurried. Inside the wrapper were three packets of hundred-rouble notes.
“It’s all there, the whole three thousand roubles. You needn’t count it. Take it,” Smerdyakov urged Ivan, with a nod at the notes. Ivan sank back into his chair. He was white as a handkerchief.
“You scared me ... with that stocking,” he said, with a strange grin.
“Can you really not have known till now?” Smerdyakov asked once more.
“No, I didn’t know. I kept thinking it was Dmitri. Brother, brother! Ach!” All at once he clutched his head in both hands.
“Listen. Did you kill him on your own? With my brother’s help, or without it?”
“Only with you, with your help, did I kill him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch is perfectly innocent.”
“All right, all right. We’ll talk about me later. Why do I keep shaking? I can’t even talk straight.”

“You were bold enough then. You said ‘everything was lawful,’ and look how frightened you are now,” Smerdyakov muttered, surprised. “Won’t you take some lemonade? I’ll ask for some at once. It’s very refreshing. Only I must hide this first.”

And again he nodded at the notes. He was about to get up and call through the door to Marya Kondratyevna to make some lemonade and bring it in. But he wanted something to cover the notes, so she wouldn’t see them. He took out his handkerchief first, and when that turned out to be very dirty, he picked up the big yellow book that Ivan had noticed on the table when he came in, and laid it over the notes. The book was _The Sayings of the Holy Father Isaac the Syrian_. Ivan read the title without thinking.
“I don’t want any lemonade,” he said. “We’ll talk about me later. Sit down and tell me how you did it. Tell me all of it.”
“You’d better take your greatcoat off, or you’ll get too hot.” As if the thought had only just struck him, Ivan took off his coat and, without getting up, threw it onto the bench.
“Speak, go on, speak.”
He seemed calmer now. He waited, sure that Smerdyakov would tell him _all_ of it.
“How it was done?” sighed Smerdyakov. “It was done in the most natural way, just as you said.”

“Never mind what I said, we’ll come to that,” Ivan cut in again, seemingly quite in command of himself, choosing his words firmly and no longer shouting as before. “Only tell me exactly how you did it. All of it, as it happened. Don’t forget anything. Above all, the details. The details, I beg you.”
“You’d gone away, and then I fell into the cellar.”
“In a fit, or a faked one?”
“Faked, naturally. I faked it all. I went quietly down the steps to the very bottom and lay down quietly, and as I lay down I screamed and thrashed about, until they carried me out.”
“Wait! And did you keep faking it all through afterward, even in the hospital?”
“No, not at all. The next day, in the morning, before they took me to the hospital, I had a real attack, worse than any I’d had in years. For two days I was out cold.”
“All right, all right. Go on.”

“They laid me on the bed. I knew I’d be on the other side of the partition, because whenever I was ill Marfa Ignatyevna put me there, close to them. She’s always been very good to me, ever since I was born. At night I moaned, but quietly. All the while I was expecting Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come.”
“Expecting him? To come to you?”

“Not to me. I expected him to come into the house. I had no doubt he’d come that night. Without me there, and with no news, he was bound to come and climb over the fence, as he used to, and do something.”
“And if he hadn’t come?”
“Then nothing would have happened. I’d never have made up my mind to it without him.”
“All right, all right ... speak more clearly, don’t rush, and above all, don’t leave anything out!”

“I expected him to kill Fyodor Pavlovitch. I thought that was certain, since I had been preparing him for it ... these last few days.... He knew about the knocks. That was the main thing. Suspicious as he is, and with the fury that had been building in him all those days, he was bound to get into the house by means of those taps. It couldn’t be avoided, so I was waiting for him.”
“Wait,” Ivan interrupted. “If he’d killed him, he would have taken the money and gone off with it. You must have thought of that. What would you have gained by it afterward? I don’t see.”

“But he’d never have found the money. That was only what I told him, that the money was under the mattress. It wasn’t true. It had been lying in a box. And afterward I suggested to Fyodor Pavlovitch, since I was the only person he trusted, that he hide the envelope with the notes in the corner behind the ikons. Nobody would have guessed that place, especially if they came in a hurry. So that’s where the envelope lay, in the corner behind the ikons. It would have been absurd to keep it under the mattress. The box, at least, could be locked. But everybody believes it was under the mattress. A stupid thing to believe. So if Dmitri Fyodorovitch had committed the murder, he’d have found nothing. He would either have run off in a hurry, scared of every sound, as murderers always are, or he would have been arrested. Either way I could have climbed up to the ikons and taken the money away the next morning, or even that very night, and it would all have been put down to Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I could count on that.”
“But what if he didn’t kill him, but only knocked him down?”

“If he hadn’t killed him, of course, I wouldn’t have dared take the money, and nothing would have happened. But I reckoned he’d beat him senseless, and then I’d have time to take it. After that I’d make out to Fyodor Pavlovitch that nobody but Dmitri Fyodorovitch had taken the money, after beating him.”
“Stop ... I’m getting confused. So it was Dmitri after all who killed him, and you only took the money?”

“No, he didn’t kill him. Well, I might as well have told you now that he was the murderer.... But I don’t want to lie to you now, because ... because if you really haven’t understood until now, as I can see for myself, and you’re not pretending, just to pin your guilt on me to my face, then you’re still responsible for everything. You knew about the murder, you ordered me to do it, and you went away knowing all about it. So this evening I mean to prove to your face that you are the only real murderer in the whole affair. I’m not the real murderer, though I did kill him. You are the rightful murderer.”

“Why, why am I a murderer? Oh, God!” Ivan cried. At last he couldn’t hold himself back, and he forgot that he had put off discussing himself until the end of the conversation. “You still mean that Tchermashnya business? Wait, tell me, why did you want my consent, if you really took Tchermashnya for consent? How can you explain that now?”

“With your consent assured, I’d have known you wouldn’t raise a cry over losing those three thousand, even if suspicion had fallen on me instead of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or on me as his accomplice. On the contrary, you’d have shielded me from others.... And once you had your inheritance, you’d have rewarded me whenever you could, for the rest of your life. For you’d have got your inheritance through me. If he had married Agrafena Alexandrovna, you wouldn’t have had a farthing.”
“Ah! So you meant to hold it over me for the rest of my life,” snarled Ivan. “And what if I hadn’t gone away then, but had informed on you?”

“What could you have informed on? That I talked you into going to Tchermashnya? That’s all nonsense. Besides, after our conversation you’d have either gone away or stayed. If you’d stayed, nothing would have happened. I’d have known you didn’t want it done, and I’d have tried nothing. Since you went away, it meant you were assuring me that you wouldn’t dare inform on me at the trial, and that you’d overlook my having the three thousand. And indeed you couldn’t have prosecuted me afterward, because then I’d have told everything in court. Not that I’d stolen the money or killed him, mind you, I wouldn’t have said that. I’d have said that you put me up to the theft and the murder, though I didn’t agree to it. That’s why I needed your consent, so you couldn’t have cornered me afterward. For what proof could you have had? I could always have cornered you, by exposing how eager you were for your father’s death. And I tell you, the public would have believed every word, and you’d have been ashamed for the rest of your life.”
“Was I so eager, then? Was I?” Ivan snarled again.

“Of course you were, and by your consent you silently approved of my doing it.” Smerdyakov looked firmly at Ivan. He was very weak and spoke slowly and wearily, but some hidden inner force drove him on. He evidently had some purpose. Ivan sensed it.
“Go on,” he said. “Tell me how that night went.”

“What is there left to tell? I was lying there, and I thought I heard the master shout. Just before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and gone out, and then he let out a scream, and after that it was all silent and dark. I lay there waiting, my heart thumping. I couldn’t stand it. In the end I got up and went out. The window on the left, the one facing the garden, was standing open. I stepped over to the left and listened for whether he was sitting in there alive, and I heard the master moving about and sighing. So I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!’ I thought. I went up to the window and called to him, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he’s run off.’ He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he said, and pointed. He was whispering too. ‘Wait a bit,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there was Grigory Vassilyevitch, lying by the wall, covered in blood and out cold. So it’s true, I thought, Dmitri Fyodorovitch really has been here. And on the spot I decided to put an end to it all. Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, would never know what happened, lying there senseless like that. The one danger was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the time. But the longing to get it done had come over me so badly that I could scarcely breathe. I went back to the window and told the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come and wants to be let in.’ And he jumped like a baby. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but he couldn’t believe it. ‘She’s standing out there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out of the window at me, half believing and half suspicious, and afraid to open. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought. And it struck me as funny. So I thought of knocking on the window frame, right there before his eyes, with those taps we had agreed on as the sign that Grushenka had come. He didn’t seem to trust my word, but the moment he heard the taps, he ran to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the doorway so I couldn’t get past. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He stared at me, shaking all over. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘if he’s that frightened of me, it looks bad!’ And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn’t let me in, or would shout, or that Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or that something else would go wrong. I can’t remember now, but I must have stood there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she’s there, right under the window; how can you not see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her.’ ‘She’s scared,’ I said; ‘the noise frightened her, she’s hiding in the bushes; go and call her yourself from the study.’ He ran to the window and put the candle on the sill. ‘Grushenka,’ he cried, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ He cried it, but he wouldn’t lean out of the window, and he wouldn’t step away from me, because he was in a panic. He was so frightened he didn’t dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, there she is,’ I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out. ‘There she is; she’s in the bush, laughing at you, can’t you see her?’ All at once he believed it. He was shaking all over—he was terribly crazy about her—and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up the iron paperweight from his table; you remember it, about three pounds in weight? I swung it and struck him on the top of the skull with the corner. He didn’t even cry out. He just sagged down, and I struck him again, and a third time. By the third blow I knew I had broken his skull. He suddenly rolled over on his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked round. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight and put it back. Then I went to the ikons, took the money out of the envelope, and flung the envelope on the floor with the pink ribbon beside it. I went out into the garden, shaking all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know the hollow. I’d marked it long before and left a rag and a scrap of paper ready inside. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and shoved it deep into the hole. And there it stayed for over two weeks. I took it out afterwards, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed and lay down, thinking, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may turn out badly for me. But if he’s not killed and he recovers, it’ll be first-rate, because then he’ll swear that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so Dmitri Fyodorovitch must have killed him and taken the money.’ Then I began to groan, from suspense and impatience, to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as I could. At last she got up and ran to me, but when she saw that Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn’t there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. That set it all in motion, and it put my mind at rest.”

He stopped. Ivan had listened the whole time in dead silence, without moving or taking his eyes off him. While telling his story, Smerdyakov had looked at him now and then, but for the most part he kept his eyes turned aside. Now that he had finished, he was plainly agitated and breathing hard. Sweat stood out on his face. Whether he felt remorse, or something else, there was no way to tell.
“Hold on,” cried Ivan, thinking hard. “What about the door? If he opened the door only for you, how could Grigory have seen it open earlier? Grigory saw it open before you went in.”

It was remarkable that Ivan spoke quite amicably now, in a different tone, not angry as before. If anyone had opened the door at that moment and looked in, he would certainly have concluded that the two were talking peacefully about some ordinary, though interesting, subject.

“As for that door, and Grigory Vassilyevitch saying he saw it open, that’s only his imagination,” said Smerdyakov with a wry smile. “He’s no man, I assure you, he’s an obstinate mule. He didn’t see it. He only fancied he’d seen it, and nothing will shake him. It’s our luck that he took that notion into his head, because after it they can’t fail to convict Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Listen ...” said Ivan, who seemed bewildered again and was struggling to catch hold of something. “Listen. There are many questions I wanted to ask you, but I’ve forgotten them ... I keep forgetting, and I get muddled. Yes. Tell me this, at least. Why did you open the envelope and leave it lying on the floor? Why didn’t you just carry the envelope off?... When you were telling me, I thought you spoke of it as if it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can’t understand....”

“I had a good reason for doing it. Take a man who knew all about the matter, as I did, for instance. Say he’d seen those notes before, and maybe had put them in that envelope himself, and had watched with his own eyes while it was sealed and addressed. If a man like that did the murder, why would he rip the envelope open afterwards, and in such desperate haste, too, when he knew for certain the notes were inside? No, if the robber were someone like me, he’d simply put the envelope straight in his pocket and be off with it as fast as he could. With Dmitri Fyodorovitch it would be quite another thing. He knew about the envelope only by hearsay; he’d never seen it. If he’d found it under the mattress, say, he’d have torn it open as fast as he could, to make sure the notes were in it. And he’d have thrown the envelope down, with no time to think that it would count as evidence against him. For he was no regular thief and had never stolen anything outright before. He’s a gentleman born. And if he did bring himself to steal, it wouldn’t be real stealing, just taking what was his own, since he’d told the whole town beforehand that he would, and had even boasted aloud before everybody that he’d go and take his property from Fyodor Pavlovitch. I didn’t say any of this openly to the prosecutor when he questioned me. On the contrary, I steered him toward it with a hint, as if I didn’t see it myself, as if he’d thought of it on his own and I hadn’t put it in his head. And Mr. Prosecutor’s mouth positively watered at my suggestion.”
“But can you really have thought all that out on the spot?” cried Ivan, overwhelmed with astonishment. He looked at Smerdyakov again, with alarm.
“Mercy on us! Could anybody think all that out in such a desperate hurry? It was all worked out beforehand.”
“Well ... well, the devil must have helped you!” Ivan cried again. “No, you’re no fool, you’re a good deal cleverer than I thought....”

He rose, evidently meaning to pace the room. He was in terrible distress. But the table stood in his way, and there was scarcely room to squeeze between the table and the wall, so he only turned around where he stood and sat down again. Perhaps not being able to move irritated him, for he suddenly burst out, almost as furiously as before.

“Listen, you wretched, contemptible creature! Do you not understand that if I haven’t killed you, it’s only because I’m saving you to answer for this tomorrow at the trial? God sees,” Ivan raised his hand, “perhaps I too was guilty. Perhaps I really did have a secret wish for my father’s ... death. But I swear I wasn’t as guilty as you suppose, and perhaps I didn’t push you into it at all. No, no, I didn’t push you into it! But no matter. Tomorrow at the trial I will testify against myself. I’m resolved on it! I will tell everything, everything. But we’ll go there together. And whatever you say against me at the trial, whatever evidence you give, I’ll stand up to it; I’m not afraid of you. I’ll confirm all of it myself! But you must confess too! You must, you must; we’ll go together. That is how it will be!”
Ivan said this solemnly and with resolve, and his flashing eyes alone were enough to show that it would be so.
“You’re ill, I can see; you’re quite ill. Your eyes have gone yellow,” Smerdyakov observed, without the slightest irony, and with what seemed real sympathy.
“We’ll go together,” Ivan said again. “And if you won’t go, never mind, I’ll go alone.”
Smerdyakov fell silent, as if considering.
“It won’t come to that, and you won’t go,” he concluded at last, flatly.
“You don’t understand me,” Ivan cried reproachfully.

“You’ll be too ashamed to confess it all. And what’s more, it will do no good whatever. I’ll say flat out that I never told you anything of the kind. I’ll say you’re either ill (and it looks that way, too), or so sorry for your brother that you’re sacrificing yourself to save him and have made it all up against me. You’ve never thought more of me than of a fly, after all. And who will believe you? What single proof do you have?”
“Listen, you showed me those notes just now to convince me.”
Smerdyakov lifted the book off the notes and put it aside.
“Take that money away with you,” Smerdyakov sighed.
“Of course I’ll take it. But why give it to me, if you did the murder for its sake?” Ivan stared at him in great surprise.

“I don’t want it,” Smerdyakov said in a shaky voice, making a gesture of refusal. “I did have the idea of starting a new life on that money, in Moscow or, better still, abroad. I dreamed of it, mostly because ‘all things are lawful.’ You were quite right in what you taught me, for you talked to me about it often enough. If there’s no everlasting God, there’s no such thing as virtue, and no need of any. You were right about that. That’s how I saw it.”
“Did you work that out for yourself?” asked Ivan, with a wry smile.
“With your guidance.”
“And now, I suppose, you believe in God, since you’re handing back the money?”
“No, I don’t believe,” Smerdyakov whispered.
“Then why are you handing it back?”

“Stop ... that’s enough!” Smerdyakov waved his hand again. “You said yourself that everything was lawful. So why are you so upset now, as well? You even want to go and testify against yourself.... Only it won’t happen! You won’t go and testify,” Smerdyakov declared with conviction.
“You’ll see,” said Ivan.

“It’s not possible. You’re very clever. You love money, I know that. You like being respected, too, because you’re very proud. You’re far too fond of women’s charms, as well, and what you care about most is living in peaceful comfort, depending on nobody. You won’t want to ruin your life forever by taking a disgrace like that on yourself. You’re like Fyodor Pavlovitch, more like him than any of his children. You have the same soul he had.”
“You’re no fool,” said Ivan, who seemed struck. The blood rushed to his face. “You’re serious now!” he remarked, looking at Smerdyakov all at once with a different expression.
“It was your pride that made you take me for a fool. Take the money.”
Ivan took the three rolls of notes and stuffed them in his pocket, without wrapping them in anything.
“I’ll show them in court tomorrow,” he said.
“Nobody will believe you. You have plenty of money of your own, and might simply have taken it from your cash-box and brought it to court.”
Ivan got up from his seat.
“I say it once more,” he said. “The only reason I haven’t killed you is that I need you tomorrow. Remember that, don’t forget it!”

“Well, kill me. Kill me now,” said Smerdyakov, all at once giving Ivan a strange look. “You won’t even dare do that!” he added with a bitter smile. “You won’t dare do anything, you, who used to be so bold!”
“Till tomorrow,” cried Ivan, and turned to go out.
“Wait a moment.... Show me those notes once more.”
Ivan took out the notes and showed them to him. Smerdyakov looked them over for ten seconds.
“Well, you can go,” he said, with a wave of the hand. “Ivan Fyodorovitch!” he called after him again.
“What is it?” Ivan answered, turning but not stopping.
“Good-bye!”
“Till tomorrow!” Ivan cried once more, and he walked out of the cottage.

The snowstorm was still raging. For the first few steps he walked boldly, but then he began to stagger. “It’s something physical,” he thought, grinning. Something like joy was welling up in his heart. He felt a boundless resolve. He would end the wavering that had tormented him so much lately. His decision was made, “and now it won’t change,” he thought with relief. Just then he stumbled over something and nearly fell. He stopped short and saw at his feet the peasant he had knocked down, still lying there senseless and motionless. The snow had almost covered his face. Ivan grabbed him and lifted him in his arms. He saw a light in the little house on the right, went over, knocked at the shutters, and asked the man who lived there to help him carry the peasant to the police station, promising him three roubles. The man got ready and came out. I won’t describe in detail how Ivan managed to get the peasant to the police station and have a doctor see him at once, and how freely he paid out for the expenses. I will say only that the business took a whole hour, and that Ivan was well pleased with it. His mind wandered and raced the whole time.

“If I hadn’t made up my mind so firmly about tomorrow,” he reflected with satisfaction, “I wouldn’t have spent a whole hour looking after that peasant. I’d have passed by without caring if he froze. And I can still watch myself, incidentally,” he thought in the same instant, with even greater satisfaction, “though they’ve decided I’m losing my mind!”

As he reached his own house, he suddenly stopped and asked himself whether he shouldn’t go at once to the prosecutor and tell him everything. He settled the question by turning back toward the house. “All of it together tomorrow!” he whispered to himself. And, strange to say, almost all his gladness and self-satisfaction vanished in a moment.

When he walked into his own room, he felt a touch of ice on his heart. It was like a memory or, more exactly, a reminder, of something agonizing and revolting that was in that room now, at this very moment, and had been there before. He sank wearily onto his sofa. The old woman brought him a samovar. He made tea but did not touch it. He sat on the sofa feeling dizzy. He felt ill and helpless. He started to doze off, but got up uneasily and paced the room to shake off the drowsiness. At times he thought he was delirious, though illness was not what he thought of most. He sat down again and began to look around, as if searching for something. This happened several times. At last his eyes fixed intently on one spot. Ivan smiled, but an angry flush spread over his face. He sat there a long time with his head propped on both arms, still glancing sideways at the same spot, at the sofa standing against the opposite wall. Something was plainly there, some object, that irritated him, worried him and tormented him.
